chapter_theme: Not giving (ஈயாமை): to cook and eat is to share; the miser who neither gives nor enjoys is mocked by his own hoard, loses it to strangers and heirs, and is worse off than the poor. Giving must be done now, in whatever measure one can, and wealth held without giving is a house of suffering.
structure_note: The chapter moves from the duty to share and to give now (271-272) to the miser's folly and loss (273-278), defines true liberality against the base man's forced yield (279), and ends with wealth itself as the dwelling of suffering (280).

271.reading: To share what is cooked, as far as one has, with friends and with those who are not friends, and then eat, is what cooking and eating means; for the worthless who shut the door and eat inside, the door of the other world is shut.
271.nuance: The punishment mirrors the fault: a shut door for a shut door. Mudaliar takes 'friends' as kin and 'not friends' as guests; Pope has 'friends and foes', which widens the duty further than either commentator.

272.reading: Those who do small acts of virtue, however little, within their means, rise; those who say they will think about it after they gain great wealth are lost in a sea of blame.
272.nuance: The verse reverses the usual excuse: it is the small giver who is great and the one waiting for great wealth who drowns. Mudaliar notes that 'are lost' is past tense for certainty.

273.reading: The fool who neither enjoys his wealth nor gives anything to renunciants, but hoards it and dies, is laughed at by the very wealth he stored, and by the compassion in the world.
273.nuance: The wealth itself is made to mock him: it outlives him and was never used. The gift named is to renunciants (துறவோர்), a pointer to the Jain setting. Shanmuganar's commentary is missing.

274.reading: The great wealth of the tight-hearted man who knows neither how to give nor how to enjoy will in due season be enjoyed by a stranger, like a lovely daughter of the house.
274.nuance: The daughter is raised in the house and goes to an outsider when she comes of age; the image makes the loss natural and certain, not a mishap.

275.reading: Though they live by the great sea with its dashing waves, people wait at a small, nearly dry well for its trickle and drink; so the deep poverty of the worthy is better than the wealth of those who know nothing of the next world.
275.nuance: The sea is plenty that cannot be used; the small well is little that can. Shanmuganar takes 'knowing the next world' as knowing and doing the good deeds that belong to it.

276.reading: The wealth the fool keeps calling 'mine, mine', I too call 'mine, mine': if it is his, he neither gives it nor enjoys it, and neither do I.
276.nuance: A joke with a sting: ownership that produces no use is no different from not owning. Shanmuganar's commentary on this quatrain appears under 275.

277.reading: The poor have escaped much that troubles the rich who do not give: being called ruined, the toil of guarding, the digging to bury it, the aching hands that clutch it; many are their escapes.
277.nuance: The list is ironic consolation, not praise of poverty: the comparison is only with the miser. Pope reads the last escape as tying it up against powerful plunderers; Mudaliar as gripping it tight.

278.reading: While it was his he did not give, and his heirs do not give once it is theirs; had he given first, they would not have stopped him, and when they give later, he cannot stop them.
278.nuance: The argument removes every excuse: nobody prevented either party from giving. Pope's added sentence states the moral, that only one's own avarice stops giving.

279.reading: Liberality is to yield gladly, as a cow does to its calf, the askers being the calf and the givers the cow; the base yield, like a cow milked by force, only when strong men press and torment them.
279.nuance: The same act, giving, is good or base by the way it comes out. Mudaliar records several readings of வாய் வைத்து: by many devices, by reviling, or with instruments. Pope's translation is missing for this quatrain.

280.reading: Gaining wealth is suffering, guarding it is bitter suffering, its dwindling is suffering and its loss is suffering: wealth is the very dwelling place of suffering.
280.nuance: The verse speaks of wealth itself, not only the miser's, though the chapter setting is not giving. Every stage, from earning to loss, is suffering, so no stage is safe. Shanmuganar's commentary is missing.

links.note: Both condemn eating alone to keep one's store full. The Kural ranks it more bitter than begging; 271 shuts the door of the next world on it.
Both reject putting virtue off: the Kural's அன்று அறிவாம் என்னாது ('without saying we'll see to it later') answers the very words of 272's delayers, பின் அறிதும்.
Both describe the man who stores wealth, does not use it and dies: the Kural says he achieved nothing, 273 that his own wealth laughs at him.

Both liken the miser's wealth to a beautiful young woman, with opposite outcomes: in the Kural she grows old alone, unused; here she is enjoyed in due season by a stranger. Unused or lost, the miser has none of it.
Both say that those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing, whatever they hold. 276 makes it a joke in which the speaker owns the miser's wealth as much as he does.
Kural 1041 says nothing is more painful than poverty. 277 names troubles poverty spares, but only in comparison with the ungiving rich, so it limits 1041 rather than contradicting it.
274 says the miser's wealth goes to a stranger; 278 follows it to the heirs, who repeat his avarice, so the wealth does no good in either generation.

Both say the base yield only when crushed: like sugar-cane (Kural), like a cow milked by force (here). Both use கொல்ல for the crushing. The Kural's worthy give at a word; here the giver yields like a cow to its calf.

Kural 754 says wealth gained by right means and without wrong yields virtue and pleasure; 280 says wealth at every stage, earning included, is the dwelling of suffering. Both speak of wealth as such and its yield. The tension holds if 280 is about wealth in general, as its wording suggests, and not only the miser's, as the chapter setting might imply.
277 lists the miser's troubles of guarding, burying and clutching; 280 generalizes them into a sequence of earning, guarding, dwindling and loss.

source_issues: Quatrain 275: Shanmuganar's field also holds the text of 276 and his commentary on it; 276's own Shanmuganar field is not aligned.
Quatrain 279: Pope's translation is not aligned, and Shanmuganar's field ends with the text of 280; Shanmuganar's commentary on 280 is missing.
